scope: Twenty-one actual, short AQA school-mock-eligible original Physics and Chemistry recall cards; 12 Physics on resolving, motion graphs, slopes and projectiles, and 9 Chemistry on mass spectrometry, ionisation, lattice formation/dissociation, weak acid and Ka. No multi-mark question disguised as a flashcard.
method: Use exact original front/back and ID guards; retain all previously accepted/rejected lists; add one clear legitimate equivalent and two clearly false misconceptions per original short card. Reject misconception exact strings before fuzzy partial-credit fallback. The runtime/CI checks verify model answers and former accepted/rejected examples survive.
limitations: New examples improve the named 21 cards but cannot guarantee every possible free-text answer is assessed perfectly.
No full AQA specification bullet or diagram/practical-skill completion is implied.
The Maths first school mock remains Year 1 Pure, while Chemistry AS plus taught A2 and Physics AS plus taught A2 remain unchanged.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: A 12 N force is 30° from the vertical. Find its horizontal and vertical components.
rows.originalBack: Horizontal = 12 sin30° = 6.0 N; vertical = 12 cos30° ≈ 10.4 N.
accept: The horizontal component is 12 sin 30° = 6.0 N, and the vertical component is 12 cos 30° = 10.4 N.
reject: Horizontal 10.4 N and vertical 6.0 N: sine and cosine are interchanged.
The horizontal and vertical components are both 12 N.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: 50 N at 30° above horizontal: find horizontal and vertical components.
rows.originalBack: Horizontal = 50 cos 30° = 43.3 N; vertical = 50 sin 30° = 25.0 N.
accept: For 50 N at 30° above horizontal, horizontal = 43.3 N and vertical = 25.0 N.
reject: Horizontal 25.0 N, vertical 43.3 N.
Horizontal 50 N, vertical 50 N.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: 50 N at 30° to vertical: find horizontal and vertical components.
rows.originalBack: Horizontal = 50 sin 30° = 25.0 N; vertical = 50 cos 30° = 43.3 N.
accept: For 50 N at 30° to vertical, horizontal = 25.0 N and vertical = 43.3 N.
reject: Horizontal 43.3 N, vertical 25.0 N.
The horizontal component is 50 N and the vertical is zero.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What does area below the time axis on an acceleration–time graph mean?
rows.originalBack: A negative change in velocity, not a negative distance. It need not mean the object slows down.
accept: A negative signed area under an acceleration-time graph means negative change in velocity, which does not necessarily mean slowing down.
reject: A negative acceleration-time area always means negative distance travelled.
A negative area always proves the object is slowing down.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What does crossing the time axis on a velocity–time graph mean?
rows.originalBack: Velocity passes through zero and changes sign: the object stops momentarily, then reverses direction.
accept: The velocity passes through zero and changes sign, so motion reverses direction at the crossing.
reject: Crossing the velocity-time axis means the displacement must be zero.
When velocity crosses zero, the acceleration must also become zero.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: A displacement–time curve has a positive gradient which becomes less steep. What happens to velocity?
rows.originalBack: Velocity remains positive but decreases: the object moves forwards while slowing down.
accept: The displacement-time gradient is still positive but is decreasing, so forward velocity becomes smaller.
reject: Velocity turns negative because the displacement-time curve gets less steep.
Positive displacement-time gradient that gets less steep means the object speeds up.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What does a horizontal velocity–time graph below the time axis show?
rows.originalBack: Constant negative velocity; acceleration is zero. The object is moving, not stationary.
accept: The object travels with steady velocity in the negative direction and zero acceleration.
reject: A flat line below zero on a velocity-time graph means the object is at rest.
The flat negative velocity-time line means constant negative acceleration.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: A 2.0 kg object accelerates at 3.0 m s⁻². Friction is 4.0 N opposite the pull. Find the pull.
rows.originalBack: Resultant force = ma = 6.0 N; pulling force = 6.0+4.0 = 10.0 N.
accept: The net force is 2.0 × 3.0 = 6.0 N; the pull must also overcome 4.0 N friction, so it is 10.0 N.
reject: The pulling force is only 6.0 N, ignoring friction.
The pull is 2.0 N after subtracting friction from ma.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: How does the normal reaction change on an incline without other perpendicular forces?
rows.originalBack: R = mg cos θ.
accept: On a slope without additional perpendicular forces, normal reaction equals mg cos θ.
reject: Normal reaction equals mg sin θ on a simple slope.
Normal reaction must be mg on every incline regardless of angle.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What is the weight component down a slope of angle θ?
rows.originalBack: mg sin θ.
accept: The component of weight parallel to and down an incline is mg sin θ.
reject: The downhill weight component is mg cos θ.
On a slope the downhill weight component is always the whole mg.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: Does the normal reaction always equal an object's weight?
rows.originalBack: No, only in certain force balances.
accept: No; the normal force only equals weight when the perpendicular forces balance that way, for instance on a level surface with no others.
reject: The normal reaction always equals mg, even on a slope.
The normal reaction is always zero if an object is stationary.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: A projectile has initial horizontal velocity 12 m s⁻¹. Without air resistance, what is its speed at the highest point?
rows.originalBack: 12 m s⁻¹.
accept: At maximum height the vertical component is zero but the 12 m s⁻¹ horizontal component remains, so speed is 12 m s⁻¹.
reject: The projectile has zero speed at its highest point.
The speed at maximum height must be 9.8 m s⁻¹.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What is formed by electron-impact ionisation of X(g)?
rows.originalBack: X⁺(g), after an electron is removed.
accept: Electron-impact ionisation removes an electron and leaves the gaseous positive ion X⁺(g).
reject: Electron impact produces only a negative ion X⁻(g).
Electron-impact ionisation leaves the particle neutral with no electron removed.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: Write the first ionisation equation for magnesium.
rows.originalBack: Mg(g) → Mg⁺(g) + e⁻.
accept: Mg(g) → Mg⁺(g) + e⁻ is the first ionisation of gaseous magnesium atoms.
reject: Mg(g) → Mg²⁺(g) + 2e⁻ is the first ionisation equation.
Mg(s) → Mg⁺(aq) + e⁻ is the standard first ionisation equation.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: Write the second ionisation equation for magnesium.
rows.originalBack: Mg⁺(g) → Mg²⁺(g) + e⁻.
accept: Mg⁺(g) → Mg²⁺(g) + e⁻ is the second ionisation of gaseous magnesium.
reject: Mg(g) → Mg⁺(g) + e⁻ is the second ionisation equation.
Mg⁺(g) → Mg²⁺(g) + 2e⁻ is the second ionisation equation.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: Why do successive ionisation energies increase?
rows.originalBack: Each electron is removed from an increasingly positive ion.
accept: Successive electrons are removed from more positively charged ions, so remaining electrons feel stronger attraction to the nucleus.
reject: Ionisation energy rises because each new electron is farther from the nucleus after removal.
Each successive electron is easier to remove because attraction falls as the ion becomes more positive.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: How many electrons can an s, p and d subshell hold?
accept: The maximum number of electrons is s = 2, p = 6 and d = 10.
reject: An s subshell holds 2, p holds 8 and d holds 10 electrons.
An s subshell holds 1, a p subshell 3 and a d subshell 5 electrons.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: Define lattice dissociation enthalpy.
rows.originalBack: The enthalpy change when 1 mole of an ionic solid is completely separated into its constituent gaseous ions.
accept: One mole of solid ionic compound separates completely into its constituent gaseous ions.
reject: Lattice dissociation enthalpy forms an ionic solid from its gaseous ions.
Lattice dissociation produces one mole of aqueous ions by dissolving the solid in water.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: How is lattice formation enthalpy related to lattice dissociation enthalpy?
rows.originalBack: Same magnitude, opposite sign.
accept: They describe reverse processes, so lattice formation has the same magnitude but the opposite sign to lattice dissociation.
reject: Lattice formation and dissociation enthalpies always have the same sign.
The magnitude of lattice formation enthalpy is twice that of dissociation for the same compound.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.sourceTopic: Strong weak acids pH Ka Kw
rows.originalFront: Why are carboxylic acids weak acids?
rows.originalBack: They only partially dissociate in water.
accept: Carboxylic acids are weak because only a fraction of their molecules dissociate to release H⁺ in water.
reject: A carboxylic acid is weak because it completely dissociates in water.
Carboxylic acids are weak because none of their molecules can release H⁺ in water.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.sourceTopic: Strong weak acids pH Ka Kw
rows.originalFront: Write the Ka expression for HA ⇌ H⁺ + A⁻.
accept: For HA ⇌ H⁺ + A⁻, Ka equals [H⁺][A⁻] divided by [HA].
reject: Ka = [HA]/([H⁺][A⁻]) for HA dissociation.
Ka = [H⁺][HA]/[A⁻] for the dissociation of HA.
